en: Petavatthu,
Cūḷavagga 5.
The Story of the Young Man’s Ghost (Kumārapetavatthu)
Wondrous is the knowledge of the Sugata,
how the Teacher has declared the individual:
some indeed become possessed of abundant merit.
There are some who possess only meager merit:
"This boy, abandoned in the charnel ground,
survives the night on the moisture from his own thumb."
Neither spirits, nor ghosts,
nor reptiles shall harm the youth who has performed meritorious deeds;
even dogs will lick his feet.
Vultures and jackals turn it over;
flocks of birds carry off the contents of the womb,
while crows carry away the impurities from the eyes.
No one provided protection for him,
neither medicine nor mustard-seed fumigation;
they did not even take recourse to the conjunctions of the constellations.
Not even all kinds of grain were scattered [to cover it].
Thus, having fallen into the utmost distress,
it was cast into the charnel ground, red with blood.
Trembling like a ball of meat thrown into a fire,
with his life remaining but uncertain— him,
who is honored by gods and men, he beheld.
Having seen him, the one of vast wisdom made this declaration:
"This prince, within this city,
will become the foremost in terms of family and wealth."
“What was the vow? And what was the holy life?
Of what well-practiced deed is this the result, that having met with such a calamity as this?”
"He will experience such [rewards] through his psychic power.
The people performed a magnificent offering for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
There, perceiving a change in his mind,
he spoke harsh and unseemly words.
Having dispelled that thought, [he said:]
Having subsequently attained joy and confidence,
she attended upon the Tathāgata as he dwelt in Jeta’s Grove for seven nights with offerings of rice gruel.
That indeed was his holy life,
and this is the result of that well-practiced conduct;
having encountered such a calamity as this, [he has attained this state].
Such success as that he shall experience.
Having remained right here for a hundred years,
endowed with all sensual pleasures;
"With the breakup of the body, in the life hereafter,
he goes to the company of Vāsava.
This is the fifth story of the young man who became a peta.
